author: sonnet
reason: Document A is the easier one to learn the system from cold: its Terms section defines every outside constraint before the steps use it (the 60 s request limit, the 512 MB workers, the attempt and retry rules, the multipart and bucket lifecycle rules), and it explains the reasons behind its choices (why there are two paths, why export state lives on the primary, why a shared row reader). Document B leaves some of these constraints implicit and refers ahead to helpers and steps defined later.

author: sonnet
reason: B is better for an outsider because it sets out the context first: what the page is, why there are two paths (the 60 s request limit and 512 MB workers), and what is out of scope; it also defines the platform constraints A only mentions in passing (read replica, keyset paging, bucket lifecycle rules, at-least-once delivery) and collects the rules that apply to every step in one place before the step-by-step walkthrough.

author: haiku
reason: A gives an unfamiliar engineer more to stand on: it starts with how the gateway works today, defines terms like EVAL, PTTL and windowIndex, includes the actual Lua script, explains why the steps run in their order, and puts every branch in the diagram (Enterprise unlimited, backend timeout), whereas B is tidier but leaves the Enterprise path and the window and expiry mechanics more abstract.

author: haiku
reason: B is easier for a newcomer to the stack: it describes the current system before the change (stateless instances behind a load balancer), says why the steps run in this order, defines EVAL, Lua and PTTL, shows the real Lua script, and also covers backend timeouts and the metrics, while A is tighter but assumes more background.

author: sonnet
reason: A defines every component a newcomer would not know (Key Service, Redis, Lua script, customer). It walks through the flow in numbered steps that match the diagram, and it lists failure behaviour in one table, so it is easier to understand the system from A without knowing the project; B is tighter but assumes more and leaves cases such as a Key Service outage out of scope.

author: sonnet
reason: For an outsider, B is the easier one to learn from: it says why Redis must be shared, explains the Key Service and Lua scripts, walks through the flow step by step against the diagram, and has a failure table that covers more cases than A's denser decision list, which assumes more background.

author: haiku
reason: A starts by explaining the current system: UserRepository, the lint rule, the version column, StaleWrite, and the load figures. It then gives a numbered four-stage overview, defines every mechanism before using it, and adds a failure table, so a newcomer can follow it on its own terms; B is tighter, but it assumes context it never gives, such as the brief, StaleWrite and how the repository works.

author: haiku
reason: B is better for a newcomer: it opens by describing the current system (UserRepository, the lint rule, row counts and load, the erasure job, the empty pg-core cluster), explains its design choices (outbox and relay, why not app.jobs, the control-row fence), and adds a failure table, whereas A is tighter but assumes you already know the project.

author: sonnet
reason: A explains how the system runs (write, delete, read and switch paths) in its own section before the rollout steps, and ends with a failure table, so a newcomer gets the whole picture in one place; B spreads those mechanics across steps 2, 3 and 9.

author: sonnet
reason: B gives the runtime mechanism its own "How the system runs" section, covering MySQL-first writes, deletes and erasure, Postgres-first writes, reads and the switch, before the rollout steps, and ends with a failure table; A spreads the same mechanism through the step list, so a newcomer has to piece the system together from the rollout sequence.

author: haiku
reason: A explains how double charges are actually prevented, using a charge-claim row with a unique constraint and a step-by-step procedure for each charge, and it defines every term it relies on; B is tidier but rests on an undefined "invoice version" key and a check-the-ledger-then-charge step that it never shows to be race-free.

author: haiku
reason: Document A is easier for a newcomer to follow: each rollback step uses the same template (what starts it, what it does, where its data lives, how it fails, when it moves on), and its single diagram shows the whole rollback path, while B's claim mechanism is more thorough but comes with denser terms, duplicated sub-state diagrams and long prose that make the system harder to grasp.

author: sonnet
reason: B is easier for a newcomer to follow: its rollback steps run in a logical order (settle, then reprocess, then reconcile), each step says what happens when it fails, and its double-charge protection is a concrete mechanism (one controller is the only writer of the flag, and a pending ledger entry is written in the same transaction as the freeze check), while A adds more terms and a nested diagram and even asks in its own open questions whether its reprocess step is needed.

author: sonnet
reason: A explains the mechanism more clearly: one controller writes the flag and enforces the gates, a pending ledger entry is written in the same transaction that checks the freeze, and the rollback steps run in a logical order (freeze, settle, reprocess, reconcile, flip), each with its failure rule. B leaves more undecided (gates checked by hand, unknown flag propagation) and puts reprocess after reconcile, then admits reprocess may not be needed.

author: haiku
reason: Document A opens with a plain summary of the whole saga, explains why the flow is shaped as it is (reserve before charging, claim only after payment), and defines every term and diagram convention, whereas B is tighter but adds branching logic (re-reserve on late success, LATE_SUCCESS, treating a missing provider record as a decline) with less explanation for a newcomer.

author: haiku
reason: B fits a newcomer better: it explains the saga and compensating-step model, says why stock is reserved before payment but claimed only after it, explains how to read the diagram, and ends with a short list of invariants, while A is tighter and covers more mechanisms but drops a reader into a dense flowchart with little framing.
